title: Sixteen-paragraph article with three scattered edits
before:
Two years ago our weekly team meeting took ninety minutes and most of it was people reading out status updates. Nobody enjoyed it, but nobody wanted to be the one to cancel it.

So we ran an experiment. For six weeks we replaced the meeting with a short written update posted every Monday morning.

The format was simple. Each person answered three questions: what did I finish, what is blocking me, and what do I need from others this week.

At first the updates were too long. People wrote essays, and nobody read them past the first paragraph.

We set a limit of one hundred and fifty words per update. It felt strict, but it forced everyone to pick what actually mattered.

Within a month the quality improved. Blockers were visible earlier, and people started replying to each other directly in the thread.

Managers were the most skeptical group. They worried they would lose touch with how people were doing.

In practice the opposite happened. A written update leaves a trail, so patterns such as repeated blockers became easy to spot.

We kept one live meeting each month, thirty minutes long, for topics that need discussion. The agenda is built from questions raised in the written threads.

Not everything worked. New joiners found the written format cold, and we had to pair each of them with a buddy for the first weeks.

Time zones were another test. Our colleagues in Vilnius read the updates in the afternoon, which meant replies often arrived the next day.

We accepted that delay. For most topics, a reply within a day is fast enough.

Urgent matters go to chat or a phone call. We agreed that the weekly update is never the place for an emergency.

After six weeks we asked everyone whether to go back to the old meeting. Not one person voted for it.

We have kept the format ever since. The Monday update is now the first thing many of us read at work.

If you want to try this, start small. Pick one team, set a word limit and run it for a month before you decide.
